title: TLS record coalescing: client flush sweep (lab notes)
content:
Summary:
Quick lab notes from a focused sweep on how small application writes + TLS record framing interact with TCP-level coalescing and proxies (especially mTLS termination at an edge proxy). We found scenarios where naive small writes per token create many small TLS records, which increases syscall count, CPU on the TLS path, and P99 tail latency when proxying through a TLS-terminating edge.

Why we care:
- In streaming inference we often flush partial tokens, or the client SDK does small writes (per-token or per-chunk).
- TLS record size and write coalescing behavior (app-level flushes + TCP_NODELAY/Nagle) change how bytes are packetized; that affects proxy CPU and queueing.
- Most prior notes focus on chunking and proxy buffering; fewer experiments isolate TLS record framing effects and simple mitigations (client-side aggregation, small changes to OpenSSL BIO flushing).

Hypotheses:
1) Many small app writes -> many small TLS records -> more send syscalls and more TLS encryption ops -> higher CPU/time-per-token and wider tail.
2) Enabling client-side write aggregation (coalesce N tokens or bytes) reduces TLS records and improves P95/P99 with modest increase in median.
3) TCP-level knobs (TCP_CORK/Nagle) interact with TLS: in many stacks TCP_CORK only helps if we delay flush until at least one TLS record boundary; otherwise TLS recordization happens earlier.
4) gRPC (HTTP/2) tends to produce smaller application writes when using streaming libraries; HTTP/1.1 chunked may behave differently depending on client lib flush patterns.

Experiment matrix (mini):
- Clients: python-requests/HTTP1 chunked, golang net/http2 (grpc-go) streaming, custom C++ client (libcurl/openssl manual flush).
- TLS stack: OpenSSL 3.0 default flush vs patched BIO that coalesces up to 8k before record.
- TCP options: default, TCP_NODELAY=1, TCP_CORK on (linux), socket-level writev aggregation (app-level).
- Proxy: envoy edge with mTLS termination -> upstream mTLS off (simulation of edge). Also a pure TCP passthrough proxy as baseline.
- Payload pattern: tokenized streaming where each token is ~10-40 bytes of payload plus JSON overhead. We used realistic prompt sizes and tokenization patterns from real workloads.

Measurement methods:
- qps: synthetic generator at 500rps and 2000rps sustained phases.
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 for first-byte and final-byte (stream end) measured at client and at proxy ingress.
- Syscalls: strace -c on client process to count send/sendmsg/writev calls per request.
- TLS records: tcpdump + tshark to extract TLS record lengths and counts per connection.
- CPU: top/perf on proxy and client.
- Network: bytes-per-packet and MSS alignment.

Key micro-scripts used (local names):
- tools/stream_gen.py (python, tokenized writes, configurable flush per token)
- tools/openssl_coalesce_patch.sh (build OpenSSL with BIO coalescing hook)
- infra/run_envoy_edge.sh (envoy config toggles: http2 max-concurrent-streams, connection buffers)
- infra/collect_tls_records.sh (tcpdump -> tshark formatting)

Representative results (selected rows, AVG over 5 runs):

Scenario | send-calls/req | tls-records/req | client CPU% | proxy CPU% | p99 latency (ms)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
small-writes + NODELAY | 42 | 38 | 18% | 34% | 243
small-writes + TCP_CORK | 12 | 11 | 10% | 18% | 132
small-writes + app-agg(8k) | 3 | 2 | 6% | 11% | 95
grpc-go-streaming (default) | 36 | 30 | 16% | 30% | 210
grpc-go + app-agg(4 tokens) | 8 | 7 | 9% | 14% | 118
http1-chunked (requests flush per write) | 40 | 37 | 17% | 32% | 220
http1 + agg-buf(linger 5ms) | 14 | 12 | 9% | 16% | 140

Notes on numbers:
- send-calls/req includes write/sendmsg syscalls used to push TLS records.
- tls-records/req counted at the network capture (post-TLS framing).
- p99 measured at client end-to-end time for the streaming response (final byte).

Interpretation and observations:
- There is a clear correlation between TLS records/req and proxy CPU and p99 latency. Many small TLS records inflate proxy-side TLS decrypt overhead and amplify queueing inside the proxy (more interrupts/context switches).
- TCP_CORK on the client is very effective when we can control write boundaries (C/C++/go). For managed runtimes (python), it's harder but we can implement short buffering (linger/flush delay) in the client to similar effect.
- Application-level aggregation (buffer N tokens or up to X bytes with max-linger 3-10ms) gives the best tradeoff: large drop in p99 while median increases only slightly (~5-12ms). For interactive use, a 5-10ms additional median is acceptable if p99 drops massively.
- gRPC libraries in go/c++ do fewer syscalls if configured for larger grpc write buffers. grpc-go currently exposes limited knobs; filing follow-up to expose an 'aggregation-window' in our SDK wrapper.
- Edge proxies amplify the problem: a TLS-terminating edge experiences larger CPU pressure when receiving many small records, which cascades into queueing delays for downstream requests (we saw queue length spikes ~2-4x).

Quick diffs vs other findings in repo:
- This doc isolates the TLS recordization layer specifically; prior docs measured chunking and proxy backpressure but didn't separate TLS-record count from application chunk count.
- Adds concrete syscall level measurements and a practical mitigation (small app-side aggregation/linger).

Actionable recommendations (provisional):
1) SDK change: Add a default client-side micro-aggregation window (configurable) in SDKs (python/js/go) to coalesce token writes into 1-4 TLS records per chunk. Default: 8k or 5 tokens or 5ms linger (whichever triggers first).
2) Best-practice doc for customers: Warn about per-token flush patterns; provide example snippet showing how to set socket options or use SDK flag to enable aggregation.
3) Edge tuning: Explore TLS worker autoscaling when many small-record workloads detected; consider fast-path on edge that accepts raw multiplexed frames to avoid per-record crypto costs.
4) Add a telemetry metric: tls_records_per_request sampled per route. Tie to alerts when tls_records_per_request > 12 for streaming routes.
5) Follow-up experiments: combined effect of TLS record size + kernel offload (TCP segmentation offload/TSO) and impact on P99 under bursty ingress (1000->5000rps spikes).

Open questions / TODOs:
- How do hardware TLS offload and kernel bypass (DPDK/AF_XDP) change the break-even point for aggregation? Early thinking: offload reduces CPU penalty, but TLS records still create per-record state in proxies. Need to test in dedicated cluster.
- Interactions with HTTP/2 flow control windows and HEAD-OF-LINE when aggregating larger records (might worsen first-byte latency for mid-stream messages in some patterns).
- UX: balance SDK defaults (we want safe opt-out but good out-of-box P99).

Raw notes / rough commands used:
- strace -f -c -e trace=write,sendto,sendmsg ./client_bin
- tcpdump -i any -w /tmp/cap.pcap tcp and port 443
- tshark -r /tmp/cap.pcap -Y "tls.record.version==0x0303" -T fields -e tls.record.length | wc -l
- perf record -p <pid> -- sleep 60; perf report

Appendix: suggested SDK snippet (python pseudo)
- class StreamClient:
    def __init__(..., agg_ms=5, agg_bytes=8192):
        self.agg_ms = agg_ms
        self.agg_bytes = agg_bytes
        self._buf = bytearray()
    def write_token(self, token_bytes):
        self._buf.extend(token_bytes)
        if len(self._buf) >= self.agg_bytes:
            self._flush()
        else:
            schedule_flush_in(self.agg_ms)

- This is intentionally simple; real implementation needs flush coalescing across asyncio/eventloop boundaries.

Conclusions:
Client-side coalescing of small writes into larger TLS records is an inexpensive and high-impact mitigation for streaming inference workloads. We should drive a cross-team effort (SDK + telemetry + edge tuning) to make this a default optimization across our hosted and dedicated deployments.

Notes to reviewers:
- Numbers are from lab env with VM-based envoy edge and moderate synthetic load. Do not treat absolute latencies as production values; look at relative improvements.
- Diego and Priya helped run the syscall captures and validate the TLS record counting.
- Linking to JIRA-RT-3421 for the SDK follow-up and GH PR stub in linked_artifacts.

-- Aisha
